strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: a unified 3D sinusoidal (Video Fourier Field) representation for continuous space-time video super-resolution, avoiding explicit warping and factorized spatial/temporal modeling.
Principled, closed-form anti-aliasing mechanism via a Gaussian PSF applied analytically to the Fourier basis — a genuinely useful and computationally cheap property that prior C-STVSR methods lack.

Extensive evaluation across multiple tasks (full C-STVSR, arbitrary-scale spatial SR on REDS, video frame interpolation, temporal consistency via tOF) and datasets (Vid4, GoPro, Adobe240, REDS), with consistent, large improvements (up to ~2 dB PSNR) over strong recent baselines including BF-STVSR and MoTIF.

Favorable efficiency profile: fastest inference time (1.27 s vs 1.88–3.03 s) and moderate VRAM compared to baselines, plus a capacity-matched comparison and a scalable Large variant showing the approach is not yet saturated.
Includes out-of-distribution evaluation (cross-dataset AVSR on REDS), retraining of baselines where needed for fairness (e.g., SAVSR on REDS), and an honest limitations section.
Method is simple, interpretable, and clearly described; implementation details (backbone, training schedule, hardware) are sufficiently complete.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: the sinusoidal basis with closed-form Gaussian PSF anti-aliasing closely follows Thera (Becker et al., 2025), here essentially lifted from 2D images to 3D (x,y,t) and combined with an off-the-shelf RVRT backbone. The paper is transparent about this, but the conceptual step is modest.

A potential confound weakens the central claim: V³ uses RVRT as backbone encoder while competing C-STVSR methods (VideoINR, MoTIF, BF-STVSR) use weaker backbones. The large PSNR gains may partly stem from the stronger backbone rather than the VFF representation itself. A controlled ablation — same RVRT encoder with a local INR or other decoder head (à la VideoINR/LIC/MoTIF style) — is missing and would be the decisive experiment.

No ablations over key design choices: number of basis functions N, voxel grid size, learned vs. per-voxel frequencies, and — importantly — the benefit of the analytical PSF sampling vs. learned/scale-agnostic sampling. The anti-aliasing advantage is asserted but never isolated experimentally.

Perceptual quality is not evaluated beyond PSNR/SSIM: no LPIPS, no user study, no temporal-flicker metrics besides tOF on Vid4 only. Given the claim of sharper reconstructions, perceptual metrics would strengthen the evidence.
Concerns about over-smoothing at high scaling factors are acknowledged but not quantified; the regression-only objective limits perceptual applicability.
No explicit code release or link is provided (project page placeholder), which limits reproducibility despite the detailed description; training requires 16 GH200 chips, a substantial compute budget.
Vid4 evaluation uses only temporal ×2 while other datasets use ×8, and Vid4 is small; some comparisons (e.g., ZoomingSloMo) have missing entries.

strengths: The core idea is conceptually clean and appealing: a unified, continuous 3D sinusoidal representation (VFF) for space-time video SR, avoiding explicit warping and decoupled spatial/temporal modeling, with a closed-form, signal-theoretically grounded Gaussian PSF for anti-aliasing (Eq. 4).

Extensive empirical evaluation: joint C-STVSR, arbitrary-scale spatial SR (in-distribution and out-of-distribution on REDS), video frame interpolation, and temporal consistency (tOF), consistently setting a new state of the art, often by >1.5 dB PSNR — a large margin for this task.
The method is also reported to be faster and more memory-efficient than recent competitors (Table 6, Fig. 1), which strengthens the practical significance of the gains.
Honest limitations section discussing over-smoothing at high scale factors and potential representational bottlenecks of a finite Fourier sum.
Supplementary AVSR-specific comparison (Table 5) against dedicated AVSR methods with re-training on matched data is a good-faith effort at fair evaluation.
weaknesses: A critical confound is not isolated: V3 uses RVRT (a strong, modern video restoration transformer) as its backbone, while all compared C-STVSR baselines use substantially lighter architectures. Matching parameter counts does not control for backbone strength. Without an ablation swapping the encoder (e.g., VFF heads on the baselines' backbones), it is unclear whether the reported 1.5–2 dB gains stem from the proposed VFF representation or simply from the stronger encoder — this weakens the central claim of the paper.

There are essentially no component-level ablations: the contribution of the PSF-aware sampling (Eq. 4), the shared fixed frequency basis vs. per-voxel frequencies, the number of basis functions N, the voxel size, and the temporal receptive field are all untested. Claims such as 'sharing frequencies improves stability' and 'hard-wiring the PSF ensures good generalization' are asserted rather than demonstrated.

The anti-aliasing advantage — presented as a key selling point — is never directly evaluated (e.g., aliasing artifacts when sampling at lower-than-trained scales or with mismatched PSFs); the evidence is only indirect via PSNR at various factors.

The representation borrows heavily from Thera (Becker et al., 2025); extending an aliasing-free sinusoidal field from 2D images to 3D video is a natural step, so the novelty, while real, is more incremental than the framing suggests.

Training uses only synthetic bicubic/subsampling degradations; robustness to realistic degradations (noise, compression, motion blur) is deferred to future work, limiting practical relevance, and only regression metrics (PSNR/SSIM/tOF) are reported — no perceptual metrics such as LPIPS.

Evaluation on Vid4 and Adobe240 follows prior work, but Vid4 has only 30 clips, and statistical significance/variance of the reported gains is not discussed; the empty 'Project page' link hurts reproducibility, and no code is stated to be released.
Minor writing/typos: 'increase' instead of 'increasing', inconsistent method naming (V3 vs. V^2.5), and an unusually short method section relative to the empirical claims.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a genuine conceptual gap in continuous space-time video super-resolution (C-STVSR), namely the decoupling of spatial and temporal modeling plus reliance on error-prone explicit warping, and proposes a unified, principled alternative.

The proposed Video Fourier Field (VFF) representation is simple, interpretable, and technically elegant: closed-form Gaussian PSF sampling for aliasing-free reconstruction at arbitrary scales (Eq. 4) is a concrete, computationally cheap mechanism that competing INR/warping-based methods lack; encoding translation as phase shifts is a natural fit for video motion.

Strong empirical results: V3 sets a new state of the art on all three standard C-STVSR benchmarks (Vid4, GoPro, Adobe240) with gains of ~1.5-2 dB PSNR over BF-STVSR/MoTIF at matched parameter counts (~14M), while being faster (1.27s) and more memory-efficient than most baselines.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: the paper covers the general C-STVSR task, the special cases of spatial-only (AVSR) and temporal-only (VFI) super-resolution, out-of-distribution scaling factors (REDS), temporal consistency (tOF metric plus qualitative temporal profiles), runtime/VRAM analysis, and a scalability check (V3-Large).
Honest limitations section discussing over-smoothing at high scales, potential representational bottleneck of the finite Fourier sum, and extension to richer degradation operators.

Reasonably good reproducibility details: implementation framework, optimizer settings, training schedule, patch sizes, hardware, and inference requirements are reported; project page is promised; a dedicated AVSR variant (V2.5) with retrained baselines (Table 5) improves fairness of comparisons.
weaknesses: Limited ablation studies: no component-wise ablations isolating the contribution of (i) the VFF representation vs. the strong RVRT backbone, (ii) the analytic PSF-aware sampling vs. learned filtering, (iii) N=512 basis functions, (iv) shared vs. per-voxel frequencies, or (v) voxel grid resolution. Since the backbone (RVRT with finetuned RAFT) already contains flow-based components, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the representation versus the encoder design or simply a stronger backbone than baselines use. This is the most significant soundness concern for attributing the ~2 dB gain to VFF specifically.

The core idea is a fairly direct 3D generalization of the 2D sinusoidal-basis approach in Thera (Becker et al., 2025) for image SR; the paper cites it for anti-aliasing but the conceptual novelty over that prior work (extending a learned sinusoidal field from 2D images to the (x,y,t) video domain) could be discussed and differentiated more carefully.

Evaluation is restricted to PSNR/SSIM and tOF; no perceptual quality metrics (LPIPS, etc.) or user study, despite claims about 'sharper' and 'visibly sharper' reconstructions. Regression-based over-smoothing at high scales is acknowledged but not quantified.

Training cost is heavy (2.5M iterations on 16x GH200 GPUs), which limits reproducibility for most labs; no released code is verifiable from the manuscript itself (project page link is empty in the text).

Some claims exceed the direct evidence: e.g., that VFF 'avoids' the error-prone warping problem is supported mostly by qualitative figures and tOF on Vid4 only; the phase-shift/translation-motion argument is asserted rather than empirically demonstrated.

Missing comparison to other recent arbitrary-scale video SR methods in the main text (they appear only in Appendix B), and ZoomingSloMo results are absent for some columns of Table 1; per-method training-protocol differences (e.g., V2.5 trained specifically on REDS vs. baselines) complicate cross-table conclusions.

Presentation issues: Figure 1's headline '2 dB' claim is based on a specific setting (Adobe240, x4/x8); the manuscript contains minor typos ('increase' in Sec. 4.1, 'accomodate', 'bases functions'), and the page-limit formatting leaves large blank spaces (pp. 14, 17).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated conceptual contribution: a unified, continuous 3D Fourier (Video Fourier Field) representation that jointly models space and time, eliminating explicit flow-based warping in continuous STVSR; the first such representation for C-STVSR as claimed.

Principled anti-aliasing mechanism: the closed-form Gaussian PSF scaling of sinusoidal basis functions (Eq. 4) is an elegant, signal-theoretically justified solution to arbitrary-scale sampling, avoiding learned ad-hoc filtering.

Very strong empirical results: new state of the art on Vid4, GoPro, and Adobe240 with ~1.5-2 dB PSNR gains, plus favorable out-of-distribution generalization to REDS and competitive results against dedicated AVSR and fixed-scale VSR methods.

Unusually thorough evaluation for this area: the paper decouples spatial-only and temporal-only SR, measures temporal consistency (tOF), analyzes learned basis functions, ablates basis size, frequency learning, and training iterations, and includes degradation robustness studies (noise, H.264 compression).
Efficiency: faster inference and lower VRAM than recent C-STVSR baselines while matching their parameter budget (~14M), with a scaling study (V3-Large).
Paper is well written and well organized, with a clear problem statement, honest limitations section, and extensive qualitative evidence in the appendix.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to PSNR/SSIM and tOF; no perceptual quality metrics (LPIPS, DISTS) or user study, which is notable given the paper claims 'sharper' reconstructions — perceptual claims rest mainly on zoomed-in qualitative figures.

Potential confound in the magnitude of the gains: V3 uses an RVRT backbone encoder (with a RAFT flow component) while compared C-STVSR baselines use lighter backbones; parameter counts are matched, but backbone capacity/receptive field differences make it hard to attribute the full ~2 dB gain to the VFF representation. A stronger ablation isolating the encoder (e.g., VFF heads on the baselines' backbones) would strengthen the causal claim.
No explicit code release is confirmed (the project page link is blank in the manuscript), which affects reproducibility; training also requires substantial compute (2.5M iterations on 16x GH200).

The representation builds directly on prior sinusoidal/anti-aliased INR work (Thera, LTE, BF-STVSR), so the novelty is primarily in the domain transfer and system integration rather than the underlying machinery; the paper acknowledges this but should more sharply delineate the delta from Thera-style heat fields.

A finite sum of sinusoids plausibly struggles with hard occlusions/disocclusions and texture discontinuities; the paper discusses this only briefly as a potential bottleneck without targeted experiments (e.g., breakdown analysis on occlusion-heavy scenes).
Minor issues: Figure 1's '2 dB' claim is specific to one setting; some ablation details (voxel size, receptive field of the coefficient head) are under-specified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine conceptual gap in continuous space-time video super-resolution: existing C-STVSR methods decouple spatial and temporal modeling and rely on explicit warping, which the authors convincingly argue is brittle. The proposed Video Fourier Field (VFF) offers a clean, unified alternative.

The anti-aliasing mechanism (closed-form Gaussian PSF applied analytically to the sinusoidal basis, Eq. 4) is theoretically principled and cheap, avoiding the need to learn scale-appropriate filtering from data.

Empirically strong and broad evaluation: new state of the art on Vid4, GoPro, and Adobe240 (up to ~2 dB PSNR), plus the special cases of AVSR (Table 2), VFI (Table 3), and standard VSR (Table 7), with favorable runtime and memory (Table 5).

Good breadth of supporting analyses: temporal consistency via tOF (Table 4), learned-basis analysis (Fig. 6), ablations on basis size, learned vs. fixed frequencies, and training iterations (Table 8), and robustness under noise and compression degradations (Table 9).
The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated problem statement, transparent implementation details, and a candid limitations section.
weaknesses: Confounding between representation and backbone: V3 uses RVRT (a strong video restoration transformer with RAFT flow) as its encoder, while baselines use substantially weaker backbones. The paper does not disentangle how much of the ~1.5-2 dB gain comes from the VFF representation versus the stronger backbone/longer training (2.5M iterations on 16 GH200s). A controlled ablation with a weaker encoder, or baselines given comparable encoders, would substantially strengthen the central claim.

Novelty relative to prior art is moderate: the core ingredient (a learned, non-orthogonal sinusoidal basis with closed-form anti-aliasing) closely follows Thera (Becker et al., 2025); the contribution is essentially porting this from images to joint (x,y,t) video space. The paper does position this, but the methodological delta is incremental.

The ablation on learned vs. fixed frequencies (Table 8, fixed ω drops to 22.85 dB on Vid4) uses a very weak strawman — a sparse uniform sampling of k-space with only 8 unique frequencies per axis — which overstates the importance of the learned basis; a denser or axis-aligned fixed basis would be a more informative control.

No perceptual quality metrics (e.g., LPIPS) in the main comparisons despite perceptual claims; evaluation is limited to PSNR/SSIM, and the authors themselves note outputs become overly smooth at high factors.

Reproducibility concerns: the project page link is empty in the manuscript, and no code or trained checkpoints are stated to be released. The extreme compute budget (2.5M iterations on 16× GH200) makes independent reproduction difficult, and the near-empty ablation at 25% of iterations suggests tuning is significant.

Some gain claims are slightly overstated: on Vid4 the improvement over BF-STVSR is ~0.9 dB rather than the >1.5 dB typical of other benchmarks, and V3-Large only marginally improves on V3, hinting the simple VFF parameterization may indeed be a representational bottleneck as the authors concede.

strengths: The proposed VFF representation is conceptually simple, elegant, and well-motivated: a joint (x,y,t) sinusoidal expansion avoids explicit warping, supports multi-frame temporal context, and enables closed-form, signal-theoretically correct anti-aliasing via an analytical Gaussian PSF (Eq. 4). This is a principled advance over prior C-STVSR methods that factor space and time and rely on learned or implicit filtering.

Strong empirical results: new state of the art on Vid4, GoPro, and Adobe240 for C-STVSR with gains of ~1-2 dB PSNR over strong recent baselines (MoTIF, BF-STVSR), while being faster (1.27 s) and using less memory than competitors.

Comprehensive and varied evaluation beyond the main task: arbitrary-scale AVSR (including out-of-distribution scaling factors), video frame interpolation, temporal consistency (tOF), robustness to noise and H.264 compression, and analysis of learned basis functions. The model gracefully handles the degenerate special cases (spatial-only/temporal-only SR) better than all baselines.

Thorough ablations in the appendix: number of basis functions N, learned vs. fixed frequencies, and training iterations. The fixed-frequency ablation (22.85 dB vs. 26.72 dB on Vid4) convincingly demonstrates the value of learning the basis, and Fig. 6 provides interpretable analysis consistent with classical Fourier theory.
Practical relevance: matched parameter count (~14M) to competitors for fair comparison, plus a scaled variant showing the approach has not saturated; inference runs on a single consumer GPU.
Clear writing, good positioning in related work (VideoINR, MoTIF, BF-STVSR), honest limitations section discussing over-smoothing and potential representational bottlenecks.
weaknesses: Attribution of gains between VFF and the backbone is not fully isolated. The model uses RVRT with RAFT as the encoder, which already provides strong multi-frame modeling; there is no ablation swapping the VFF head for an INR/decoupled head on the same backbone, so the contribution of the representation itself versus the powerful encoder (and its large receptive field) is partly inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

The abstract/project-page link is empty ('Project page: .') and no code release is explicitly stated, which weakens reproducibility for a method whose training requires 2.5M iterations on 16 GH200 GPUs.

Evaluation relies on PSNR/SSIM and tOF only; no perceptual metrics (LPIPS, tLP) or user study. The authors acknowledge the over-smoothing limitation, but quantitative perceptual evidence would strengthen the 'sharper reconstructions' claim.

Some claims are slightly overstated or under-supported: e.g., 'first such model for video super-resolution' and the superiority of unified modeling would benefit from more direct evidence (e.g., a warping-based variant with identical encoder) beyond cross-method comparisons.

During training the temporal subsampling is fixed while spatial scaling is randomized; the generalization behavior for temporal factors different from the training distribution (beyond the tested x8/x2) is not explored.
Details on how voxel-boundary continuity behaves quantitatively (potential blocking artifacts at cell boundaries) are only discussed qualitatively via the backbone's receptive field.
